CORRECTION vs the prior edition: item #1's 'toughest sanctions in history' quote and the China-Gulf-energy framing were previously attributed to a Sunday interview — an adversarial verifier traced them to Bessent's Thursday 20 Aug CNBC interview instead; his genuinely Sunday-dated remarks were a Financial Times op-ed ('economic D-Day'). The Monday 2pm ET press-conference time has also been public since Friday 21 Aug, not first disclosed Sunday. Both corrected below. items.headline: Iran sanctions rollout lands Monday 2pm ET: Bessent's genuinely-Sunday FT op-ed ('economic D-Day') adds to Thursday's harder CNBC rhetoric, as Iran's security chief threatens to shut Hormuz
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent published a Sunday 23 Aug Financial Times op-ed calling Monday's rollout an 'economic D-Day' and 'the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary.' The harder-edged quotes circulating this week — 'toughest sanctions in history' and the explicit call for China's cooperation, noting China gets ~50% of its energy from the Gulf — actually trace to Bessent's Thursday 20 Aug CNBC interview, not a Sunday one; the Monday 2pm ET Treasury press conference has been publicly scheduled since Friday 21 Aug. Over the weekend, Iran's hardline security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to halt Hormuz oil flow if Gulf states join the US crackdown, and Iran's parliament advanced a draft law to charge transit fees on ships passing the Strait — genuine counter-escalation layered on top of the sanctions rollout.
items.actionable: The Monday 2pm ET press conference is now the dated, concrete catalyst for the gold hedge and oil-linked names; Iran's Hormuz-shutdown threat and transit-fee law raise (not lower) the odds of a disorderly reaction. Keep the precious-metals sleeve sized for continued volatility into and through the announcement.

items.headline: US Treasury doubles long-end bond buybacks — the single biggest cross-asset catalyst of the week
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent announced the Treasury is at least doubling its liquidity-support buyback operations for 10-30yr securities (from $2bn to $4bn per operation), starting 9 Sep, after the 30yr yield hit a post-2007 high (~5.33%) on federal-debt concerns. Gross US national debt officially crossed $40 trillion on 20 Aug — the fastest trillion-dollar increment on record, just five months after $39T — with debt-service costs now exceeding the defense budget. The buyback announcement pulled the 10yr to 4.647% and the 30yr to 5.196%, and was widely read as a return to monetary accommodation.
items.actionable: This buyback remains the common thread behind the week's gold/silver breakout, the KOSPI round-trip, and the Bitcoin surge — a liquidity/debasement trade, not a growth story. Supportive for the silver/gold miners sleeve and the big-cash-pile thesis as real yields fall.

items.headline: Oil gives back part of Friday's Iran-sanctions rally at Sunday's Globex reopen, ahead of PCE and Warsh
items.summary: After settling Friday at Brent $94.39 (+0.65%, +6.4% on the week) and WTI $87.06 (+0.26%, +5.7% on the week) on anticipation of Monday's sanctions, oil opened the new week lower at Sunday's Globex reopen — Brent slipped below $92, WTI toward $86 — as traders take profits ahead of this week's US PCE print and Warsh's Friday Jackson Hole keynote. A separate report of a further ~2% spike on 'unconfirmed reports of Iranian tanker strikes' had an ambiguous/unverifiable dateline and is not included here.
items.actionable: Don't chase Friday's spike into Monday's Asia open — the pullback suggests the market wants to see the actual sanctions detail (2pm ET Monday) before re-testing $95 Brent; oil/gold correlation has been tight this week on the same Iran/debasement axis.

items.headline: Bitcoin gives back roughly a third of Friday's surge over the weekend — thin liquidity, not a reversal
items.summary: Bitcoin closed Friday 21 Aug at $78,335.19 (+7.26%), its best weekly performance since 2024, on over $4bn of liquidated shorts and a record $606mn single-day spot-ETF inflow (83% into BlackRock's IBIT). Over the weekend it pulled back to roughly $76,000-77,000 (a live level, not a session close, since crypto trades continuously) on thin weekend liquidity and elevated long positioning; Ethereum eased to ~$2,387-2,515 and XRP to ~$1.45-1.50, both still up sharply on the week.
items.actionable: The ETF-inflow and short-squeeze mechanics argue the underlying leg is more durable than a pure sentiment spike, but expect continued weekend-to-weekday chop; it remains a levered, correlated extension of the same liquidity/debasement trade driving gold, not a diversifier. Next catalysts: Nvidia earnings Wed 26 Aug and Jackson Hole Fri 28 Aug.

items.headline: Gold/silver breakout extends into Friday: gold hits a three-month high as the rally proves durable, not a one-off
items.summary: Gold and silver rallied sharply (GLD +3.84%, SLV +4.47%) Wed 19 Aug as the Treasury buyback news pulled real yields down ahead of the FOMC minutes release, while a weaker dollar amplified gains for foreign buyers; miners outperformed (GDX +9.42%, SILJ +9.55%, Barrick +8.82%). The move continued into Friday 21 Aug, with GLD closing at $423.36 (+1.95%), a three-month high, on continued dollar weakness and the fresh $40T debt milestone. COMEX/GLD/SLV are closed over the weekend, so no fresher close exists.
items.actionable: Confirms this is a genuine, multi-day rates/debasement-driven breakout rather than a one-off headline spike. Monday's Iran-sanctions announcement (item #1) and Jackson Hole (item #9) are the next two dated catalysts that could extend or test the move.

items.headline: KOSPI's near-perfect 2-day round trip explained: chip-stock crash (Wed) then buyback-fueled rebound (Thu), followed by a calmer profit-taking Friday
items.summary: KOSPI fell 5.80% Wed 19 Aug (Samsung -7.82%, SK Hynix -9.75%) on a US 30-year Treasury yield spike plus a Philadelphia Semiconductor Index selloff, then surged 5.89% Thu 20 Aug (nearly erasing the drop) after Samsung and SK Hynix announced massive capital-return plans and the Treasury buyback eased bond-yield fears. Friday 21 Aug was calmer: KOSPI +0.88% to 6,912.95, with retail booking profits for a second straight day while institutions were modest net buyers and foreigners net sold in aggregate despite buying over ₩430bn of Samsung specifically.
items.actionable: A leveraged, yield-driven chip-sector round trip, not a structural anomaly — a preview of how violently HK tech (Tencent/SMIC) can swing on the same yield/AI-capex-jitters axis heading into Nvidia's Wed earnings.

items.headline: Rare-earth names reverse sharply higher (MP +9.10%, UUUU +8.92%) on G7 non-China supply-chain push and US government-backed financing
items.summary: Friday's rare-earth rally reversed Thursday's AI-fear-driven selloff on three concrete policy catalysts: G7 leaders agreed to cut reliance on non-bloc (i.e. China) rare-earth suppliers, the Pentagon backed a $500M loan to Phoenix Tailings, and the Department of Energy selected seven critical-mineral processing/battery projects for support. Materials was the S&P 500's strongest sector on the day (+2.09%); MP separately reported Q2 revenue +89% YoY to $108.5M with government price-protection now 14% of revenue.
items.actionable: A genuine, government-policy-driven catalyst distinct from Thursday's sentiment-only selloff — Monday's Iran-sanctions rollout explicitly names China as a secondary target, adding a fresh sympathy-trade angle to the ex-China rare-earth re-rating thesis even though the direct catalyst is unrelated.

items.headline: Thursday's US equity selloff (S&P -0.87%, VIX +7.52%) driven by AI-capex balance-sheet fears — Nvidia's Wed earnings is now the direct test
items.summary: The WSJ flagged roughly $3 trillion of off-balance-sheet AI infrastructure commitments across nine major tech names, reviving 'AI bubble' concerns even as the 30yr yield eased post-buyback. VIX jumped over 7% to 16.01 before fully reversing Friday. Nvidia reports FQ2 earnings Wednesday 26 Aug after the close — the cleanest single read on whether this capex-fatigue narrative is real; separately, Nvidia is providing up to $105B of financing for an OpenAI Ohio data center, a sign capex intensity is still accelerating, a mild counterweight heading into the print.
items.actionable: An AI-capex-credibility scare, structurally different from the week's rates-driven metals rally — the fact it fully reversed Friday suggests it was sentiment-driven, but Wednesday's Nvidia print is the concrete near-term test.

items.headline: Jackson Hole Symposium (27-29 Aug) — Warsh previews his first keynote as 'structural, not near-term guidance', stacking with Iran sanctions and Nvidia earnings into a three-catalyst week
items.summary: Jackson Hole runs 27-29 Aug (theme: financial innovation/payments), with Kevin Warsh delivering his first keynote as Fed Chair Fri 28 Aug — 19 days before the 16 Sep FOMC decision. Warsh, confirmed 54-45 (the closest Fed Chair confirmation vote in US history), told reporters his remarks will focus on 'long-term structural questions, not near-term guidance' — tempering (not eliminating) hawkish-surprise risk versus a BofA survey pricing a broadly neutral-tone consensus. This now stacks with Monday's Iran-sanctions rollout and Wednesday's Nvidia earnings into the most catalyst-dense week since the Aug 19-20 selloff.
items.actionable: Three back-to-back binary catalysts (Iran Mon, Nvidia Wed, Warsh Fri) argue for sizing gold/silver-miner, tech and crypto-adjacent positioning for continued volatility rather than a clean directional bet on any single one resolving the current 'tentative risk rebound' regime.

items.headline: Alibaba fiscal Q1: revenue beats, profit misses on 75% YoY AI capex surge; rare HK$10.4bn southbound outflow
items.summary: Alibaba reported revenue of RMB268.95bn (+9% YoY, beat) but adjusted net profit of RMB20.72bn missed estimates as capex hit RMB67.68bn (+75% YoY) on AI infrastructure spend. Mainland investors made contrarian net additions to Alibaba (HK$2.21bn) even as Hong Kong saw a rare HK$10.4bn single-day southbound net outflow that same session — still the latest confirmed southbound print as of this run (a fresher 21 Aug figure could not be sourced, see flows-investors.json).
items.actionable: The AI-capex-driven margin compression mirrors the US 'off-balance-sheet AI commitments' scare playing out in HK tech — the contrarian mainland dip-buying is worth tracking as a read on HK tech risk appetite generally.

items.headline: Singapore banks post record/near-record Q2 2026 profits; OCBC crosses S$30 for the first time
items.summary: DBS (S$3.08bn, +9%), OCBC (S$2.22bn, +22%, record) and UOB (S$1.48bn, +10%) all beat estimates, driven by fee/wealth-management income rather than lending margins. OCBC and DBS trade at all-time highs; UOB lags on NIM compression (1.74%, -8bp), cut fee-income guidance, and is divesting UOB Asset Management.
items.actionable: SGX bank strength (OCBC/DBS momentum) is a structural positive for the owner's largest exposure sleeve independent of this week's volatility; UOB's relative weakness warrants closer monitoring versus peers.

items.headline: OCBC Research turns selective on S-REITs as the sector lags the bank-led STI sharply YTD
items.summary: OCBC Group Research maintained a selective stance on S-REITs, citing rate-hike concerns and elevated long-end yields; the iEdge S-REIT Index has returned -3.3% YTD versus +26.8% for the STI, a gap driven almost entirely by the bank rally. Top picks flagged: CapitaLand Ascendas REIT, CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust, Keppel DC REIT, CapitaLand India Trust.
items.actionable: Quantifies a divergence already implicit in this book — SGX banks near record highs while REITs lag badly on rate concerns. If adding to the SGX REIT sleeve, this argues for being selective (data-centre/industrial names) rather than broad REIT beta.
